The Crucible: Fear, Accusation and Integrity

Arthur Miller, The Crucible, 1953 · Anglais · Première et Terminale (lycée général et technologique), bac pro · Six lessons

1. Axe du programme

Programme d’anglais du lycée général et technologique, BO n° 22 du 29 mai 2025, en vigueur en Première et en Terminale depuis la rentrée 2026.

ClasseAxe principalAxes possibles aussi
PremièreAxe 3. Art et pouvoir. Arthur Miller répond au maccarthysme par le théâtre : une pièce sur 1692 devient un contre-pouvoir en 1953, et l’auteur lui-même refuse de « name names » devant la HUAC en 1956.Axe 2. Diversité et inclusion : les premiers accusés de Salem sont pauvres, isolés ou esclaves, comme Tituba ; la pièce montre comment une communauté fabrique ses boucs émissaires.
TerminaleAxe 1. Espace privé et espace public. Une faute privée, l’adultère de Proctor, devient une affaire publique ; sa confession doit être clouée à la porte de l’église, et il meurt pour garder son nom.Axe 5. Citoyenneté et mondes virtuels : la rumeur et le lynchage en ligne aujourd’hui (lesson 6). Axe 3. Fictions et réalités : une fiction tirée de procès réels, et une allégorie des années 1950. Axe 2. Territoire et mémoire : Salem réhabilite ses condamnés en 1711, puis la dernière en 2022.
LLCER anglaisTerminale : thématique « Arts et débats d’idées », axe « Art et contestation » (Miller contre la HUAC).Première : thématique « Rencontres », axe « Relation entre l’individu et le groupe » (Proctor face au village et au tribunal).
Bac proLe programme de langues vivantes de la voie professionnelle (BO spécial n° 5 du 11 avril 2019) n’impose pas d’axe : la séquence en travaille la dimension culturelle (une grande œuvre et une page d’histoire du monde anglophone) et prépare l’oral de l’examen (prise de parole en continu à partir d’un document, puis échange).Lien possible avec l’enseignement moral et civique et le programme de français de la voie professionnelle : la rumeur, la justice, le harcèlement en ligne.

2. Problématique

How can fear turn a community against its own members, and what does it cost to keep one’s integrity? Comment la peur peut-elle retourner une communauté contre ses propres membres, et que coûte le fait de rester intègre ?

Lesson 1: What really happened in Salem in 1692, and why did a whole community believe in witches? · Lesson 2: How do fear and rumour turn neighbours into accusers? · Lesson 3: Who holds power in the courtroom, and why is it impossible to prove one’s innocence? · Lesson 4: Why does John Proctor choose to die rather than sign a lie? · Lesson 5: Why did Arthur Miller use 1692 to speak about the America of the 1950s? · Lesson 6: Are social media pile-ons a modern witch hunt?

3. Objectifs linguistiques

  • The passive to tell history: was accused, were hanged (lesson 1).
  • Reporting a rumour: they say that, apparently, it is rumoured that (lesson 2).
  • The language of the court: I swear that, I object, I beg you to, either … or (lesson 3).
  • Regret and past hypothesis: could have, should have, if he had … he would have (lesson 4).
  • Comparing two periods: like, as, both, similarly, whereas (lesson 5).
  • Conceding and giving advice: admittedly, however, you should, before sharing (lesson 6).
  • Language activities : compréhension de l’écrit (documents historiques, extraits de la pièce, essai de Miller), expression orale en continu (flash d’information, exposé de deux minutes), interaction orale (assemblée du village, procès, débat), expression écrite (journal, lettre, plaidoyer ou tribune).

4. Ancrage culturel

Les procès de Salem (1692) et la colonie puritaine du Massachusetts ; le sermon de Jonathan Edwards (1741) ; Arthur Miller, The Crucible (1953) ; la peur rouge, Joseph McCarthy, la HUAC, la liste noire d’Hollywood, Edward R. Murrow ; Miller devant la HUAC (1956) et son essai « Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’ » (The New Yorker, 1996) ; le film de Nicholas Hytner (1996) ; les réhabilitations de 1711 et de 2022 ; la rumeur en ligne et le 3018. Œuvres : Noble, Matteson, Grant Wood.

5. Niveau CECRL

  • Première : B1+ vers B2.
  • Terminale LV1 : B2 vers C1, avec un parcours C1/C2 à chaque lesson.
  • Bac pro (Version B) : B1, six lessons plus courtes.
  • Dys-friendly version : B1, six lessons, une étape à la fois.

PREMIÈRE · UPPER SECONDARY · B1+ towards B2

The Crucible: Fear, Accusation and Integrity

Key question: How can fear turn a community against its own members, and what does it cost to keep one's integrity?

Axes: Fictions et réalités · Espace privé et espace public · Art et pouvoir · Citoyenneté et mondes virtuels.

The play: Arthur Miller's The Crucible opened on Broadway on 22 January 1953. It stages the Salem witch trials of 1692 and was written during the hunt for communists in the United States.

Final task (written expression, choose one): John Proctor's written plea to the court, or an op-ed about rumour and public shaming today (300 words).

Intermediary tasks: a radio news flash from Salem (oral), a town meeting (interaction), a courtroom scene in your own words (interaction), a two minute exposé (oral production), a class debate (interaction).

Easy to find: The Crucible (1996), directed by Nicholas Hytner, with Daniel Day-Lewis, Winona Ryder and Joan Allen, screenplay by Arthur Miller. Good Night, and Good Luck (2005), directed by George Clooney, with David Strathairn as Edward R. Murrow.

Watch the film at home

The Crucible (1996), directed by Nicholas Hytner. In France, the film is called La Chasse aux sorcières.

  1. Where to watch: see the list of streaming and rental options on JustWatch France.
  2. DVD: ask at your local library or médiathèque.
  3. Official trailer: on the Apple TV page of the film.
  4. Scenes to watch: Act I: the girls dance in the forest at night (the opening of the film). Act II: the officers arrest Elizabeth at home. Act III: in court, the girls turn against Mary Warren. Act IV: Proctor tears his confession and walks to the gallows.

Watch with English subtitles if you can.

PREMIÈRE · UPPER SECONDARY · B1+ towards B2

Lesson 1: Salem, 1692: the real story

Part 1. What really happened in Salem in 1692, and why did a whole community believe in witches?

Objectives

  • Understand the historical context of the Salem witch trials
  • Use past tenses and passive forms to tell real events
  • Give a short oral news flash

Warm-up

Image analysis: a mysterious American couple. Who are these people? What do they value? What might they fear? What links can you see with the strict world of Salem?

Students see the word witch hunt. In pairs: what does it mean today? Where have you heard it? Then: what was a real witch hunt?

Documents

Document 1: Salem Village, 1692.
  • Salem is a Puritan community in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Life is strict, winters are hard, and neighbours quarrel over land.
  • In early 1692, two girls in the house of the minister Samuel Parris, his daughter Betty and his niece Abigail Williams, start having strange fits. A doctor suggests an "evil hand".
  • The first three women accused are Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne and Tituba, an enslaved woman in the Parris household. Tituba confesses and names others.
  • A special court, the Court of Oyer and Terminer, is set up in 1692. It accepts "spectral evidence": a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her.
  • More than 200 people are accused. Nineteen are hanged, among them the farmer John Proctor in August 1692. Giles Corey, who refuses to plead, is pressed to death under heavy stones. Several others die in jail.
  • In 1711, the colony reverses many convictions and pays compensation. In 2022, Massachusetts officially cleared the last convicted woman, Elizabeth Johnson Jr.
Easy to find: "What really happened during the Salem Witch Trials", Brian A. Pavlac, TED-Ed.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: Salem, 1692: the real story

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 1 “Salem Village, 1692”, with Jonathan Edwards, “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” (1741)

  • “In early 1692, two girls in the house of the minister Samuel Parris, his daughter Betty and his niece Abigail Williams, start having strange fits.” (Document 1)
  • “It accepts “spectral evidence”: a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her.” (Document 1)
  • “More than 200 people are accused. Nineteen are hanged” (Document 1)
  • “The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you” (Jonathan Edwards, sermon, 8 July 1741)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 1What strikes you first?
Two girls of the minister’s house “start having strange fits”, and “A doctor suggests an ‘evil hand’” (Document 1).
The mystery starts in the most respected house of the village, and the first explanation offered is the Devil.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 1Which clues? In which line?
“The first three women accused are Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne and Tituba, an enslaved woman in the Parris household” (Document 1).
The first accused are poor, isolated or enslaved: the weakest are blamed first. They are scapegoats.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDoc. 1What effect? What contrast?
The court “accepts ‘spectral evidence’: a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her” (Document 1).
A vision that nobody else can see becomes proof: the accused can prove nothing against it, so the trials can only go on.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 1What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the colony will quickly admit that the trials were wrong.
Partly confirmed: “In 1711, the colony reverses many convictions and pays compensation”, but the last convicted woman, Elizabeth Johnson Jr., was cleared only “In 2022” (Document 1).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningDoc. 1Which interpretation do I defend?
A world of sin and hellfire (“over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider”, Edwards, 1741), hard winters, quarrels over land, and a court that accepts visions (Document 1).
Belief came from faith, fear and interest together: a strict community found in witches both an explanation and a scapegoat.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 1: Salem, 1692: the real story · Dys-friendly version

Question: What really happened in Salem in 1692, and why did a whole community believe in witches?

Four words:

  • accused: said to be guilty of a crime
  • hanged: killed with a rope around the neck
  • spectral evidence: a vision of a spirit used as proof in court
  • Puritan: a strict Protestant of the 1600s

One line to read: “In early 1692, two girls in the house of the minister Samuel Parris, his daughter Betty and his niece Abigail Williams, start having strange fits.” (Document 1)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

  • “The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you” (Jonathan Edwards, sermon, 8 July 1741)

Activities

  1. Timeline: put eight events in order and justify with a connector (first, then, as a result, eventually).
  2. Grammar: the passive to tell history. Sarah Good was accused. Nineteen people were hanged. The convictions were reversed.
  3. Who were the accused? Students notice that the first women accused were poor, isolated or enslaved. What does this tell us about scapegoats?
  4. Intermediary task (oral production): you are a reporter in Salem in 1692. Record a 1 minute radio news flash.

More activities

Pre-reading: a Puritan sermon

Jonathan Edwards preached this sermon in 1741, half a century after Salem, but it shows the Puritan vision of sin and God.

"The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you, and is dreadfully provoked; his wrath towards you burns like fire"
Jonathan Edwards, "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God", sermon preached at Enfield, Connecticut, 8 July 1741 (public domain)
  1. Underline the images of fire and danger. What do they make the listener feel?
  2. Find the simile. What is the sinner compared to? Why this animal?
  3. Which verbs and adjectives show God's anger?
  4. Quickwrite (five minutes): how would a community that hears such sermons every week react to a rumour of witchcraft?
Sentence starters
  • The image of... suggests that...
  • Edwards compares the sinner to... in order to...
  • The word choice creates a feeling of...
  • A community that hears this every week would...
Answer key
  1. fire, the pit of hell, wrath that burns
  2. a spider or a loathsome insect: small, helpless, disgusting
  3. abhors, dreadfully provoked, wrath, burns
  4. Open answer: fear, guilt, readiness to see the Devil everywhere.

Game: How Puritan are you? (Salem, 1692)

Imagine you are a villager in Salem in 1692. This quiz is about the period, not about your own life. Answer yes or no for your character, then count the points.

  1. Your character works hard six days a week and rests on the Sabbath.
  2. Your character goes to the meeting house every Sunday for a sermon of several hours.
  3. Your character dances in the forest at night.
  4. Your character reads the Bible at home with the family.
  5. Your character wears bright colours and lace to show off.
  6. Your character reports a neighbour who misses church.

Score: one point for each yes to questions 1, 2, 4, 6 and for each no to questions 3 and 5. The higher the score, the more your character fits the strict rules of Salem. Then discuss: was it easy to be a good Puritan? What happened to people who did not fit?

Puritanism stations

Groups move around four tables, five minutes each, and fill in a note sheet: one fact, one keyword, one question.

  1. Faith: Puritans wanted to purify the Church of England. Many sailed from England to build a godly community in New England; the Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1630.
  2. The Sabbath: Sunday is a day of rest and prayer. Work, games and travel are forbidden. Absence from church is noticed.
  3. Community and control: the church and the law are closely linked. Neighbours watch each other, and sin is a public matter.
  4. Punishment: public punishments such as the stocks shame wrongdoers in front of everyone. Reputation is everything.

Pairs: Student A is a reporter from Boston, Student B is a Salem villager in 1692. The reporter asks about the girls, the accused and the court. The villager answers, frightened and convinced.

Gap-fill worksheet

  2. Betty Parris and Abigail Williams started having strange ______.

  5. More than 200 people were ______.

  7. A ______ is a person blamed for the problems of a group.

Answer key
  1. Puritan
  2. fits
  3. confessed
  4. spectral evidence
  5. accused
  6. hanged
  7. scapegoat
  8. compensation

Lesson 2: Acts I and II: fear spreads

Part 2. How do fear and rumour turn neighbours into accusers?

Objectives

  • Understand the plot and characters of Acts I and II
  • Analyse how fear and personal grudges fuel accusations
  • Take part in a town meeting

Warm-up

Chain whisper: the teacher whispers a sentence to one student, it travels across the class. Compare the first and last versions. What changed, and why?

Documents

Document 2: the story so far. Reverend Parris finds his daughter Betty, his niece Abigail and other girls dancing in the forest at night. Betty falls ill. Rumours of witchcraft spread. Abigail once worked for John and Elizabeth Proctor, and had an affair with John; Elizabeth dismissed her. Reverend Hale, an expert in witchcraft, arrives. The girls start naming names. In Act II, Elizabeth is accused, and the clerk Cheever comes to arrest her.
"Is the accuser always holy now? Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers?"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible (1953), Act II, John Proctor
"We are what we always were in Salem, but now the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom, and common vengeance writes the law!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act II, John Proctor

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Acts I and II: fear spreads

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Arthur Miller, The Crucible (1953), Acts I and II, with Document 2 “the story so far”

  • “Is the accuser always holy now? Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers?” (Act II, John Proctor)
  • “We are what we always were in Salem, but now the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom, and common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II, John Proctor)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 2What strikes you first?
Parris “finds his daughter Betty, his niece Abigail and other girls dancing in the forest at night”, and “Rumours of witchcraft spread” (Document 2).
A small forbidden secret becomes a rumour, and the rumour grows faster than the truth.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 2Which clues? In which line?
Abigail “had an affair with John; Elizabeth dismissed her” (Document 2); the Putnams want land and influence.
Behind the accusations lie jealousy, love and land: private motives wear the mask of religion.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandAct IIWhat effect? What contrast?
Personification and metaphor: “the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom, and common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II).
Proctor sees that children now hold the keys of heaven and that private revenge has become the law: justice is turned upside down.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictAct II, then IIIWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Proctor’s question, “Is the accuser always holy now?” (Act II), will make the court doubt the girls.
Not confirmed: in Act III the court believes the girls, and Danforth warns that “a person is either with this court or he must be counted against it” (Act III).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningActs I, IIWhich interpretation do I defend?
Rumour, old grudges and fear: “common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II).
Miller shows a mechanism: fear gives power to the accusers, and each neighbour can settle an old quarrel by naming a name.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 2: Acts I and II: fear spreads · Dys-friendly version

Question: How do fear and rumour turn neighbours into accusers?

Four words:

  • rumour: a story that spreads without proof
  • grudge: an old feeling of anger against someone
  • vengeance: revenge, punishing someone for a wrong
  • jealous: unhappy because someone has what you want

One line to read: “Is the accuser always holy now? Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers?” (Act II, John Proctor)

Steps: 1. Read the line aloud. 2. Learn the four words. 3. Do the spiral below, one step at a time. 4. Say your answer with the support sentence.

Lesson 3: Act III: the court

Part 3. Who holds power in the courtroom, and why is it impossible to prove one's innocence?

Objectives

  • Understand the courtroom scene of Act III
  • Analyse power and reputation
  • Re-enact the scene in your own words

Warm-up

Image analysis: a real trial in Salem. George Jacobs, an old man, was accused in 1692. Who is accusing him? How does the painter show the courtroom and the crowd?

Students imagine a trial where the judge says: "If you are innocent, you have nothing to fear." Is this fair? Why or why not?

Documents

Document 3: Act III. Mary Warren, the Proctors' servant, comes to court with John to admit that the girls were pretending. Deputy Governor Danforth refuses to doubt the court. To destroy Abigail's credibility, Proctor confesses his affair. Elizabeth, who has never lied, is called to confirm it, but she lies to protect her husband's name. Abigail and the girls turn against Mary, who accuses Proctor. Hale denounces the court and leaves.
"It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, Mary Warren to Deputy Governor Danforth
"A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between."
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, Deputy Governor Danforth
"Private vengeance is working through this testimony!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, Reverend Hale

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Act III: the court

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, with Document 3

  • “It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits” (Act III, Mary Warren to Deputy Governor Danforth)
  • “A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between.” (Act III, Deputy Governor Danforth)
  • “Private vengeance is working through this testimony!” (Act III, Reverend Hale)
  • “A fire, a fire is burning! I hear the boot of Lucifer, I see his filthy face! And it is my face, and yours, Danforth!” (Act III, John Proctor)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeAct IIIWhat strikes you first?
Mary Warren confesses: “It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits” (Act III).
The truth finally reaches the court: it was a game that grew out of control.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesAct IIIWhich clues? In which line?
Danforth: “A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between” (Act III).
With either … or, Danforth leaves no room for doubt: every question becomes an attack on the court.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandAct IIIWhat effect? What contrast?
Proctor: “I hear the boot of Lucifer, I see his filthy face! And it is my face, and yours, Danforth!” (Act III).
Proctor turns the accusation of the Devil against the judges and against himself: everyone is guilty, the court too.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictAct IIIWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Elizabeth, who has never lied, will confirm the affair and save John.
Not confirmed: “she lies to protect her husband's name” (Document 3), and Hale cries “Private vengeance is working through this testimony!” before he leaves (Act III).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningAct IIIWhich interpretation do I defend?
Spectral evidence, “there be no road between” (Act III), and Elizabeth’s lie (Document 3).
In a court that cannot admit a mistake, a lie saves you and the truth condemns you: power belongs to the accusers and to judges who protect their own authority.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Lesson 4: Act IV: Because it is my name!

Part 4. Why does John Proctor choose to die rather than sign a lie?

Objectives

  • Understand the end of the play
  • Explore integrity, honour and public image
  • Present a two minute exposé

Warm-up

Students complete: "My name means... to me." Then: what is a reputation? Can you lose it in one day?

Documents

Document 4: Act IV. Autumn 1692. Abigail has run away with Parris's money. Rebecca Nurse and John Proctor are to be hanged. Hale begs the prisoners to confess and live. Proctor first agrees to confess, but when Danforth wants his signed confession nailed to the church door, he tears the paper. He goes to his death; Elizabeth refuses to plead with him to change his mind.
"Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, John Proctor
"How may I live without my name? I have given you my soul; leave me my name!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, John Proctor

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 4: Act IV: Because it is my name!

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, with Document 4

  • “Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!” (Act IV, John Proctor)
  • “How may I live without my name? I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” (Act IV, John Proctor)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 4What strikes you first?
“Proctor first agrees to confess, but when Danforth wants his signed confession nailed to the church door, he tears the paper” (Document 4).
The turning point is not the confession itself but its public use: his name on the church door.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesAct IVWhich clues? In which line?
Repetition: “Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!” (Act IV).
The name is his identity, his honour and what he leaves to his sons: he has only one.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandAct IVWhat effect? What contrast?
Contrast: “I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” (Act IV).
He gives up his soul to a lie, then refuses to give his name: reputation becomes integrity, the refusal to betray himself and the others.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 4What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Elizabeth will beg him to sign and live.
Not confirmed: “Elizabeth refuses to plead with him to change his mind” (Document 4).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningAct IVWhich interpretation do I defend?
“How may I live without my name?” (Act IV).
Proctor, a flawed man, becomes a tragic hero: he chooses death rather than a public lie that would betray the other prisoners and himself.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Doc. 4): “Proctor first agrees to confess, but when Danforth wants his signed confession nailed to the church door, he tears the paper” (Document 4). The turning point is not the confession itself but its public use: his name on the church door.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Act IV): Repetition: “Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!” (Act IV). The name is his identity, his honour and what he leaves to his sons: he has only one.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Act IV): Contrast: “I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” (Act IV). He gives up his soul to a lie, then refuses to give his name: reputation becomes integrity, the refusal to betray himself and the others.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Doc. 4): Hypothesis: Elizabeth will beg him to sign and live. Not confirmed: “Elizabeth refuses to plead with him to change his mind” (Document 4).
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Act IV): “How may I live without my name?” (Act IV). Proctor, a flawed man, becomes a tragic hero: he chooses death rather than a public lie that would betray the other prisoners and himself.

Lesson 5: Salem and McCarthyism

Part 5. Why did Arthur Miller use 1692 to speak about the America of the 1950s?

Objectives

  • Understand McCarthyism and the HUAC
  • Read short extracts from Miller's 1996 essay
  • Compare Salem and the Red Scare

Warm-up

Students see the word blacklist. What could it mean? What would happen to you if your name were on it?

Documents

Document 5: the Red Scare.
  • After 1945, the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union creates a fear of communist spies.
  • In February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy claims he has a list of communists working in the State Department.
  • The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) questions writers, actors and directors. They are asked to "name names". Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood.
  • In March 1954, the journalist Edward R. Murrow criticises McCarthy on his CBS programme See It Now. In December 1954, the Senate censures McCarthy.
  • In June 1956, Arthur Miller appears before HUAC and refuses to name others. He is convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957; the conviction is overturned in 1958.
"“The Crucible” was an act of desperation."
Arthur Miller, “Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’”, The New Yorker, October 1996
"Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth."
Arthur Miller, “Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’”, The New Yorker, October 1996
Easy to find: "What is McCarthyism? And how did it happen?", Ellen Schrecker, TED-Ed; the film Good Night, and Good Luck (2005).

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 5: Salem and McCarthyism

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 5 “the Red Scare”, with Arthur Miller, “Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’”, The New Yorker, October 1996

  • “They are asked to “name names”. Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood.” (Document 5)
  • ““The Crucible” was an act of desperation.” (Arthur Miller, The New Yorker, 1996)
  • “Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth.” (Arthur Miller, The New Yorker, 1996)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 5What strikes you first?
HUAC questions writers, actors and directors: “They are asked to ‘name names’” (Document 5).
Like the girls of Salem, witnesses must accuse others to save themselves.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 5Which clues? In which line?
“Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood” (Document 5).
Refusing costs a career, as refusing to confess cost a life in Salem: the pressure is the same.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandMiller, 1996What effect? What contrast?
“‘The Crucible’ was an act of desperation” (Miller, 1996).
Miller could not attack McCarthy openly, so he wrote an allegory: 1692 lets him speak about the 1950s.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 5What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Miller, like Proctor, will refuse to name others.
Confirmed: “In June 1956, Arthur Miller appears before HUAC and refuses to name others”; he is convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, and the conviction is overturned in 1958 (Document 5).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningDoc. 5Which interpretation do I defend?
“Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth” (Miller, 1996).
The allegory makes the mechanism visible (fear, accusation, forced confession) and keeps the memory of fear alive for readers who never felt it.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 5: Salem and McCarthyism · Dys-friendly version

Question: Why did Arthur Miller use 1692 to speak about the America of the 1950s?

Four words:

  • Red Scare: the fear of communism in the United States
  • blacklist: a list of people refused work
  • name names: to give the names of other people
  • censured: officially criticised

One line to read: “They are asked to “name names”. Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood.” (Document 5)

Activities

More activities

Web enquiry: McCarthyism

In pairs, use reliable sites (encyclopaedias, museums, newspapers) to answer. Note the source of each answer.

  2. What does HUAC stand for?

  5. When was McCarthy censured by the Senate?

Answer key
  1. In Wheeling, West Virginia; he claimed to have a list of communists in the State Department.
  2. House Un-American Activities Committee.
  3. Ten Hollywood screenwriters and directors who refused to answer HUAC in 1947 and were jailed and blacklisted.
  4. "Have you no sense of decency, sir?" (9 June 1954).
  5. On 2 December 1954.
  6. Elia Kazan.

Lesson 6: Witch hunts today: rumour and public shaming

Part 6. Are social media pile-ons a modern witch hunt?

Objectives

  • Discuss rumour, online pile-ons and public shaming
  • Debate with nuance and respect
  • Prepare the final task

Warm-up

Students react to the phrase "trial by social media". What is the court? Who are the judges? Is there a defence?

Class rule: we talk about public figures, fictional characters and documented cases only. Nobody shares a personal story, a name or a screenshot about themselves or anyone they know.

Documents

Document 6: the pile-on. A pile-on happens when thousands of people attack one person online at the same time, often after one post or one video taken out of context. Screenshots spread faster than corrections. Some people lose their job or leave social media, even when the accusation is later proved false. Others say public criticism holds powerful people to account.
Document 7: how to stop a rumour. Check the source. Look for the full context. Do not share, do not comment, do not add a laugh. Report harassment. Support the target in private. In France, cyberharassment is a criminal offence, and students can call 3018, the national number against online harassment.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 6: Witch hunts today: rumour and public shaming

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 6 “the pile-on” and Document 7 “how to stop a rumour”, with The Crucible, Act II

  • “A pile-on happens when thousands of people attack one person online at the same time, often after one post or one video taken out of context.” (Document 6)
  • “Screenshots spread faster than corrections.” (Document 6)
  • “Others say public criticism holds powerful people to account.” (Document 6)
  • “Check the source. Look for the full context. Do not share, do not comment, do not add a laugh. Report harassment.” (Document 7)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 6What strikes you first?
“thousands of people attack one person online at the same time” (Document 6).
As in the Salem crowd, the group gives power to each accuser and leaves the target alone.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 6Which clues? In which line?
“one post or one video taken out of context”; “Screenshots spread faster than corrections” (Document 6).
A screenshot without context works like spectral evidence: a fragment taken as proof.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDoc. 6What effect? What contrast?
“Some people lose their job … even when the accusation is later proved false”, but “public criticism holds powerful people to account” (Document 6).
The contrast brings nuance: criticism can be useful; punishment without proof is not.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 7What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: nothing can stop a pile-on.
Not confirmed: “Check the source. Look for the full context. Do not share” and “Report harassment” (Document 7). In France, cyberharassment is a criminal offence, and 3018 is the national number against online harassment.
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningDocs 6, 7Which interpretation do I defend?
“common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II) and “Screenshots spread faster than corrections” (Document 6).
The mechanism is the same (fear, a crowd, a fragment taken as proof), but today laws, journalists and bystanders can act: the play asks each of us to be the one who checks.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 6: Witch hunts today: rumour and public shaming · Dys-friendly version

Question: Are social media pile-ons a modern witch hunt?

Four words:

  • pile-on: many people attacking one person online
  • viral: spreading very fast online
  • context: the situation around words or images
  • bystander: a person who sees something and does nothing

One line to read: “A pile-on happens when thousands of people attack one person online at the same time, often after one post or one video taken out of context.” (Document 6)

  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Doc. 6): “one post or one video taken out of context”; “Screenshots spread faster than corrections” (Document 6). A screenshot without context works like spectral evidence: a fragment taken as proof.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Doc. 6): “Some people lose their job … even when the accusation is later proved false”, but “public criticism holds powerful people to account” (Document 6). The contrast brings nuance: criticism can be useful; punishment without proof is not.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Doc. 7): Hypothesis: nothing can stop a pile-on. Not confirmed: “Check the source. Look for the full context. Do not share” and “Report harassment” (Document 7). In France, cyberharassment is a criminal offence, and 3018 is the national number against online harassment.
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Docs 6, 7): “common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II) and “Screenshots spread faster than corrections” (Document 6). The mechanism is the same (fear, a crowd, a fragment taken as proof), but today laws, journalists and bystanders can act: the play asks each of us to be the one who checks.
Check my quick check
  1. pile-on
  2. viral
  3. screenshot
  4. context
  5. bystander
  6. harassment
  7. report
  8. accountable

Text study

The extract

"Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life! Because I lie and sign myself to lies! Because I am not worth the dust on the feet of them that hang! How may I live without my name? I have given you my soul; leave me my name!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, John Proctor to Deputy Governor Danforth, who wants his signed confession to be nailed to the church door.
Glossary: sign myself to lies: put my name on a lie · dust: tiny dirt · them that hang: the people who are executed · soul: spiritual self

Questions

  1. Situate the extract: who speaks, to whom, at what moment?
  2. Find the anaphora. What is its effect?
  3. Why is his name so important to him?
  4. Explain the antithesis between "soul" and "name".
  5. How is this scene a turning point?
  6. Link the extract to the McCarthy era.
Sentence starters
  • This extract takes place...
  • The repetition of 'Because'...
  • His name represents...
  • By tearing the paper, Proctor...
  • This echoes Miller's own refusal to...
Answer key (suggested answers)
  1. John Proctor, to Danforth, in Act IV, just after signing a false confession that Danforth wants to post on the church door.
  2. "Because" is repeated four times: it builds an emotional climax and shows his inner struggle.
  3. It is his identity, his reputation and the legacy he leaves to his children; signing would betray the innocent who die.
  4. He has confessed to God (soul) but refuses to let his public honour (name) be used as a lie.
  5. He tears the confession and chooses death: he recovers his integrity.
  6. Like Miller before HUAC, Proctor refuses to give his name to a lie or to blacken others.

Commentary

Write a commentary (300 words): "How does Miller make Proctor's final choice heroic?" Introduction, two parts (the language of emotion; the meaning of the name), conclusion.

Oral questioning

How it works

The teacher, or a student, asks the questions. Answer in full sentences, then ask a follow-up question to your partner. Change roles every three questions.

Questions to answer orally

  1. Where and when does the play take place?
  2. Why does Abigail accuse Elizabeth?
  3. What is spectral evidence?
  4. Why does Elizabeth lie in court?
  5. Why does Hale change his mind?
  6. Why did Miller write the play in the 1950s?
  7. Why does Proctor tear his confession?
  8. What is a modern witch hunt?
Model answers
  1. In Salem, Massachusetts, in 1692.
  2. She is jealous and wants to take her place with John Proctor.
  3. A girl claims to see the spirit of the accused attacking her; nobody else can see it.
  4. To protect her husband's reputation; tragically, it destroys his defence.
  5. He sees that private vengeance drives the accusations, and he denounces the court.
  6. To denounce McCarthyism and the HUAC hearings, where people were asked to name names.
  7. He refuses to lose his name and to betray the others who die innocent.
  8. A collective accusation without proof, for example an online pile-on.

Figures of speech

Toolbox

Figures of speech: metaphor, simile, personification, rhetorical question, antithesis, anaphora, repetition, hyperbole, irony, imperative

Identify the figure of speech

Name the main figure of speech in each line and explain its effect in one sentence.

  1. Is the accuser always holy now? (Proctor, Act II)
  2. Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers? (Proctor, Act II)
  3. the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom (Proctor, Act II)
  4. common vengeance writes the law! (Proctor, Act II)
  5. the whole world cried spirits, spirits (Mary Warren, Act III)
  6. a person is either with this court or he must be counted against it (Danforth, Act III)
  7. Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life! (Proctor, Act IV)
  8. I have given you my soul; leave me my name! (Proctor, Act IV)
  9. Fear doesn't travel well (Miller, 1996)
Sentence starters
  • This is a... because...
  • The effect is to...
  • It makes the audience feel...
  • The image suggests that...
Answer key
  1. Rhetorical question: Proctor attacks the idea that accusers are automatically innocent.
  2. Simile and irony: the accusers are compared to something pure, which mocks their claim to innocence.
  3. Metaphor: the girls now hold the power of the state and of heaven.
  4. Personification: vengeance becomes a lawmaker; private grudges have replaced justice.
  5. Hyperbole and repetition: the panic spread everywhere; collective hysteria.
  6. Antithesis and false dilemma: no neutral position is allowed.
  7. Anaphora (repetition of "Because") and exclamation: intense emotion and determination.
  8. Antithesis (soul and name) and imperative: he gives up his life but keeps his honour.
  9. Personification: fear is like a traveller; it does not survive the passing of time.

Punctuation

Punctuation reminders

Capital letters start sentences and names. A comma separates items and clauses. A question mark ends a question; an exclamation mark shows strong emotion. Quotation marks frame the words someone says. The apostrophe shows possession (Proctor's name) or a missing letter (don't).

Punctuate the sentences

Copy each sentence and add capital letters and punctuation.

  1. is the accuser always holy now
  2. because it is my name
  3. abigail parris and the other girls danced in the forest
  4. proctor asks danforth to release his wife
  5. elizabeths lie destroys johns defence
  6. hale says i denounce these proceedings
  7. salem tituba and spectral evidence are key words of act one
  8. when the trials ended many families had lost everything
Answer key
  1. Is the accuser always holy now? (Proctor, Act II)
  2. Because it is my name! (Proctor, Act IV)
  3. Abigail, Parris's niece, and the other girls danced in the forest.
  4. Proctor asks Danforth to release his wife.

Summative test

Summative test

Answer all questions. Marked out of 20: questions 1 to 4, 2 points each; questions 5 and 6, 3 points each; question 7, 6 points.

  1. When and where did the witch trials take place? (2)
  2. Who is Tituba? (2)
  3. What is HUAC and what did it ask witnesses to do? (2)
  4. Why did Miller call the play "an act of desperation"? (2)
  5. Identify and explain the figure of speech in "common vengeance writes the law". (3)
  6. Compare Hale in Act I and Act IV. (3)
  7. Essay question (150 words): "In Salem, reputation is more important than truth." Discuss. (6)
Answer key and marking
  1. In Salem, Massachusetts, in 1692.
  2. An enslaved woman in Reverend Parris's household, among the first accused; she confesses.
  3. The House Un-American Activities Committee; it asked them to name names.
  4. Because he wrote it in the climate of fear of the McCarthy era, when many were silenced.
  5. Personification: vengeance becomes a lawmaker; private grudges have replaced justice.
  6. From a proud expert hunting the Devil to a broken man begging prisoners to confess to save their lives.
  7. Marking: clear thesis (2), two arguments with examples (2), language (2). Ideas: Parris, Danforth, Elizabeth's lie, Proctor's name.

Written assessments

Assessment 1: character development

Prompt (300 words): How does John Proctor change from Act I to Act IV? Show his flaws, his turning points and his final choice.

Sentence starters
  • At the beginning of the play, Proctor is...
  • His first turning point comes when...
  • In Act III, he finally...
  • By the end, he has become...
  • This change shows that...
CriteriaLevel 1Level 2Level 3Level 4
Answer to the promptOff topicPartialClearClear and nuanced
Evidence from the playNoneGeneralPrecise examplesPrecise examples and a quotation
OrganisationNo planBasicParagraphs and connectorsFluent and logical
LanguageMany errorsSome errorsFew errorsAccurate and varied
Model answer (extract)

At the beginning of the play, John Proctor is a respected farmer who hides a guilty secret: his affair with Abigail. He despises hypocrisy, yet he is a hypocrite himself, and his silence allows Abigail to gain power. His first turning point comes in Act II, when Elizabeth is arrested: he tears the warrant and accuses the court of vengeance. In Act III, he sacrifices his reputation by confessing his adultery in public, in order to save his wife. Finally, in Act IV, he refuses to let his false confession be nailed to the church door, because his name is the only thing he still owns. Proctor moves from private guilt to public integrity; Miller shows that a flawed man can become a tragic hero.

Assessment 2: theme and Miller's purpose

Prompt (300 words): "The Crucible is not only about 1692." Discuss, using one theme (fear, reputation or power) and Miller's purpose in writing the play.

Sentence starters
  • Miller sets his play in 1692, but...
  • The theme of... appears when...
  • Like the court of Salem, HUAC...
  • Miller's purpose is to warn us that...
  • Today, this warning still matters because...
CriteriaLevel 1Level 2Level 3Level 4
Answer to the promptOff topicPartialClearClear and nuanced
Evidence from the playNoneGeneralPrecise examplesPrecise examples and a quotation
OrganisationNo planBasicParagraphs and connectorsFluent and logical
LanguageMany errorsSome errorsFew errorsAccurate and varied
Model answer (extract)

Although The Crucible takes place in Salem in 1692, Miller wrote it in the early 1950s, when HUAC asked Americans to name names. The theme of fear links the two periods: in Salem, the court sees doubt as an attack, and in the 1950s, refusing to cooperate could cost a career. Miller himself refused to name others in 1956. His purpose is to show how fear destroys justice when accusation becomes proof. The play remains relevant today, as rumours spread online faster than corrections.

The Crucible: Fear, Accusation and Integrity

Key question: How can fear turn a community against its own members, and what does it cost to keep one's integrity?

The play: Arthur Miller's The Crucible opened on Broadway on 22 January 1953. It stages the Salem witch trials of 1692 and was written during the hunt for communists in the United States.

Lesson 1: Salem, 1692: the real story

Part 1. What really happened in Salem in 1692, and why did a whole community believe in witches?

Objectives

  • Understand the historical context of the Salem witch trials
  • Use past tenses and passive forms to tell real events
  • Give a short oral news flash

Warm-up

Image analysis: a mysterious American couple. Who are these people? What do they value? What might they fear? What links can you see with the strict world of Salem?

Students see the word witch hunt. In pairs: what does it mean today? Where have you heard it? Then: what was a real witch hunt?

Documents

Document 1: Salem Village, 1692.
  • Salem is a Puritan community in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Life is strict, winters are hard, and neighbours quarrel over land.
  • In early 1692, two girls in the house of the minister Samuel Parris, his daughter Betty and his niece Abigail Williams, start having strange fits. A doctor suggests an "evil hand".
  • The first three women accused are Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne and Tituba, an enslaved woman in the Parris household. Tituba confesses and names others.
  • A special court, the Court of Oyer and Terminer, is set up in 1692. It accepts "spectral evidence": a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her.
  • More than 200 people are accused. Nineteen are hanged, among them the farmer John Proctor in August 1692. Giles Corey, who refuses to plead, is pressed to death under heavy stones. Several others die in jail.
  • In 1711, the colony reverses many convictions and pays compensation. In 2022, Massachusetts officially cleared the last convicted woman, Elizabeth Johnson Jr.
Easy to find: "What really happened during the Salem Witch Trials", Brian A. Pavlac, TED-Ed.

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 1: Salem, 1692: the real story

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 1 “Salem Village, 1692”, with Jonathan Edwards, “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” (1741)

  • “In early 1692, two girls in the house of the minister Samuel Parris, his daughter Betty and his niece Abigail Williams, start having strange fits.” (Document 1)
  • “It accepts “spectral evidence”: a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her.” (Document 1)
  • “More than 200 people are accused. Nineteen are hanged” (Document 1)
  • “The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you” (Jonathan Edwards, sermon, 8 July 1741)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 1What strikes you first?
Two girls of the minister’s house “start having strange fits”, and “A doctor suggests an ‘evil hand’” (Document 1).
The mystery starts in the most respected house of the village, and the first explanation offered is the Devil.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 1Which clues? In which line?
“The first three women accused are Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne and Tituba, an enslaved woman in the Parris household” (Document 1).
The first accused are poor, isolated or enslaved: the weakest are blamed first. They are scapegoats.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandDoc. 1What effect? What contrast?
The court “accepts ‘spectral evidence’: a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her” (Document 1).
A vision that nobody else can see becomes proof: the accused can prove nothing against it, so the trials can only go on.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 1What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: the colony will quickly admit that the trials were wrong.
Partly confirmed: “In 1711, the colony reverses many convictions and pays compensation”, but the last convicted woman, Elizabeth Johnson Jr., was cleared only “In 2022” (Document 1).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningDoc. 1Which interpretation do I defend?
A world of sin and hellfire (“over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider”, Edwards, 1741), hard winters, quarrels over land, and a court that accepts visions (Document 1).
Belief came from faith, fear and interest together: a strict community found in witches both an explanation and a scapegoat.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

More activities

Pre-reading: a Puritan sermon

Jonathan Edwards preached this sermon in 1741, half a century after Salem, but it shows the Puritan vision of sin and God.

"The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you, and is dreadfully provoked; his wrath towards you burns like fire"
Jonathan Edwards, "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God", sermon preached at Enfield, Connecticut, 8 July 1741 (public domain)
  1. Underline the images of fire and danger. What do they make the listener feel?
  2. Find the simile. What is the sinner compared to? Why this animal?
  3. Which verbs and adjectives show God's anger?
  4. Quickwrite (five minutes): how would a community that hears such sermons every week react to a rumour of witchcraft?
Sentence starters
  • The image of... suggests that...
  • Edwards compares the sinner to... in order to...
  • The word choice creates a feeling of...
  • A community that hears this every week would...
Answer key
  1. fire, the pit of hell, wrath that burns
  2. a spider or a loathsome insect: small, helpless, disgusting
  3. abhors, dreadfully provoked, wrath, burns
  4. Open answer: fear, guilt, readiness to see the Devil everywhere.

Game: How Puritan are you? (Salem, 1692)

Imagine you are a villager in Salem in 1692. This quiz is about the period, not about your own life. Answer yes or no for your character, then count the points.

  1. Your character works hard six days a week and rests on the Sabbath.
  2. Your character goes to the meeting house every Sunday for a sermon of several hours.
  3. Your character dances in the forest at night.
  4. Your character reads the Bible at home with the family.
  5. Your character wears bright colours and lace to show off.
  6. Your character reports a neighbour who misses church.

Score: one point for each yes to questions 1, 2, 4, 6 and for each no to questions 3 and 5. The higher the score, the more your character fits the strict rules of Salem. Then discuss: was it easy to be a good Puritan? What happened to people who did not fit?

Puritanism stations

Groups move around four tables, five minutes each, and fill in a note sheet: one fact, one keyword, one question.

  1. Faith: Puritans wanted to purify the Church of England. Many sailed from England to build a godly community in New England; the Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1630.
  2. The Sabbath: Sunday is a day of rest and prayer. Work, games and travel are forbidden. Absence from church is noticed.
  3. Community and control: the church and the law are closely linked. Neighbours watch each other, and sin is a public matter.
  4. Punishment: public punishments such as the stocks shame wrongdoers in front of everyone. Reputation is everything.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Doc. 1): Two girls of the minister’s house “start having strange fits”, and “A doctor suggests an ‘evil hand’” (Document 1). The mystery starts in the most respected house of the village, and the first explanation offered is the Devil.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Doc. 1): “The first three women accused are Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne and Tituba, an enslaved woman in the Parris household” (Document 1). The first accused are poor, isolated or enslaved: the weakest are blamed first. They are scapegoats.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Doc. 1): The court “accepts ‘spectral evidence’: a girl says she sees the spirit of the accused attacking her” (Document 1). A vision that nobody else can see becomes proof: the accused can prove nothing against it, so the trials can only go on.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Doc. 1): Hypothesis: the colony will quickly admit that the trials were wrong. Partly confirmed: “In 1711, the colony reverses many convictions and pays compensation”, but the last convicted woman, Elizabeth Johnson Jr., was cleared only “In 2022” (Document 1).
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Doc. 1): A world of sin and hellfire (“over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider”, Edwards, 1741), hard winters, quarrels over land, and a court that accepts visions (Document 1). Belief came from faith, fear and interest together: a strict community found in witches both an explanation and a scapegoat.

Lesson 2: Acts I and II: fear spreads

Part 2. How do fear and rumour turn neighbours into accusers?

Objectives

  • Understand the plot and characters of Acts I and II
  • Analyse how fear and personal grudges fuel accusations
  • Take part in a town meeting

Warm-up

Chain whisper: the teacher whispers a sentence to one student, it travels across the class. Compare the first and last versions. What changed, and why?

Documents

Document 2: the story so far. Reverend Parris finds his daughter Betty, his niece Abigail and other girls dancing in the forest at night. Betty falls ill. Rumours of witchcraft spread. Abigail once worked for John and Elizabeth Proctor, and had an affair with John; Elizabeth dismissed her. Reverend Hale, an expert in witchcraft, arrives. The girls start naming names. In Act II, Elizabeth is accused, and the clerk Cheever comes to arrest her.
"Is the accuser always holy now? Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers?"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible (1953), Act II, John Proctor
"We are what we always were in Salem, but now the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom, and common vengeance writes the law!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act II, John Proctor

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 2: Acts I and II: fear spreads

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Arthur Miller, The Crucible (1953), Acts I and II, with Document 2 “the story so far”

  • “Is the accuser always holy now? Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers?” (Act II, John Proctor)
  • “We are what we always were in Salem, but now the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom, and common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II, John Proctor)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 2What strikes you first?
Parris “finds his daughter Betty, his niece Abigail and other girls dancing in the forest at night”, and “Rumours of witchcraft spread” (Document 2).
A small forbidden secret becomes a rumour, and the rumour grows faster than the truth.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 2Which clues? In which line?
Abigail “had an affair with John; Elizabeth dismissed her” (Document 2); the Putnams want land and influence.
Behind the accusations lie jealousy, love and land: private motives wear the mask of religion.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandAct IIWhat effect? What contrast?
Personification and metaphor: “the little crazy children are jangling the keys of the kingdom, and common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II).
Proctor sees that children now hold the keys of heaven and that private revenge has become the law: justice is turned upside down.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictAct II, then IIIWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Proctor’s question, “Is the accuser always holy now?” (Act II), will make the court doubt the girls.
Not confirmed: in Act III the court believes the girls, and Danforth warns that “a person is either with this court or he must be counted against it” (Act III).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningActs I, IIWhich interpretation do I defend?
Rumour, old grudges and fear: “common vengeance writes the law!” (Act II).
Miller shows a mechanism: fear gives power to the accusers, and each neighbour can settle an old quarrel by naming a name.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 2: Acts I and II: fear spreads · Dys-friendly version

Question: How do fear and rumour turn neighbours into accusers?

Four words:

  • rumour: a story that spreads without proof
  • grudge: an old feeling of anger against someone
  • vengeance: revenge, punishing someone for a wrong
  • jealous: unhappy because someone has what you want

One line to read: “Is the accuser always holy now? Were they born this morning as clean as God's fingers?” (Act II, John Proctor)

Lesson 3: Act III: the court

Part 3. Who holds power in the courtroom, and why is it impossible to prove one's innocence?

Objectives

  • Understand the courtroom scene of Act III
  • Analyse power and reputation
  • Re-enact the scene in your own words

Warm-up

Image analysis: a real trial in Salem. George Jacobs, an old man, was accused in 1692. Who is accusing him? How does the painter show the courtroom and the crowd?

Students imagine a trial where the judge says: "If you are innocent, you have nothing to fear." Is this fair? Why or why not?

Documents

Document 3: Act III. Mary Warren, the Proctors' servant, comes to court with John to admit that the girls were pretending. Deputy Governor Danforth refuses to doubt the court. To destroy Abigail's credibility, Proctor confesses his affair. Elizabeth, who has never lied, is called to confirm it, but she lies to protect her husband's name. Abigail and the girls turn against Mary, who accuses Proctor. Hale denounces the court and leaves.
"It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, Mary Warren to Deputy Governor Danforth
"A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between."
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, Deputy Governor Danforth
"Private vengeance is working through this testimony!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, Reverend Hale

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 3: Act III: the court

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act III, with Document 3

  • “It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits” (Act III, Mary Warren to Deputy Governor Danforth)
  • “A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between.” (Act III, Deputy Governor Danforth)
  • “Private vengeance is working through this testimony!” (Act III, Reverend Hale)
  • “A fire, a fire is burning! I hear the boot of Lucifer, I see his filthy face! And it is my face, and yours, Danforth!” (Act III, John Proctor)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeAct IIIWhat strikes you first?
Mary Warren confesses: “It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits” (Act III).
The truth finally reaches the court: it was a game that grew out of control.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesAct IIIWhich clues? In which line?
Danforth: “A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between” (Act III).
With either … or, Danforth leaves no room for doubt: every question becomes an attack on the court.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandAct IIIWhat effect? What contrast?
Proctor: “I hear the boot of Lucifer, I see his filthy face! And it is my face, and yours, Danforth!” (Act III).
Proctor turns the accusation of the Devil against the judges and against himself: everyone is guilty, the court too.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictAct IIIWhat is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Elizabeth, who has never lied, will confirm the affair and save John.
Not confirmed: “she lies to protect her husband's name” (Document 3), and Hale cries “Private vengeance is working through this testimony!” before he leaves (Act III).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningAct IIIWhich interpretation do I defend?
Spectral evidence, “there be no road between” (Act III), and Elizabeth’s lie (Document 3).
In a court that cannot admit a mistake, a lie saves you and the truth condemns you: power belongs to the accusers and to judges who protect their own authority.
Link the analysis to the key question.

No. She lies to protect him.

The court never admits a mistake.

Activities

  1. Read the three quotations. Who speaks? What does each one show about power in the court?

Close reading: Proctor in court

Proctor's outburst at the end of Act III.

  1. Who is Proctor accusing in this speech? Only Danforth?

  3. Do the spirale de Gorse: copy the five steps on your worksheet (or use the worksheet of this lesson). For each step, write one idea and one line from the text. Then check below.

    • Proctor decides to ______ his affair.

    • Elizabeth lies to protect her husband’s ______.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Act III): Mary Warren confesses: “It were only sport in the beginning, sir, but then the whole world cried spirits, spirits” (Act III). The truth finally reaches the court: it was a game that grew out of control.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Act III): Danforth: “A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it, there be no road between” (Act III). With either … or, Danforth leaves no room for doubt: every question becomes an attack on the court.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Act III): Proctor: “I hear the boot of Lucifer, I see his filthy face! And it is my face, and yours, Danforth!” (Act III). Proctor turns the accusation of the Devil against the judges and against himself: everyone is guilty, the court too.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Act III): Hypothesis: Elizabeth, who has never lied, will confirm the affair and save John. Not confirmed: “she lies to protect her husband's name” (Document 3), and Hale cries “Private vengeance is working through this testimony!” before he leaves (Act III).
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Act III): Spectral evidence, “there be no road between” (Act III), and Elizabeth’s lie (Document 3). In a court that cannot admit a mistake, a lie saves you and the truth condemns you: power belongs to the accusers and to judges who protect their own authority.

Lesson 4: Act IV: Because it is my name!

Part 4. Why does John Proctor choose to die rather than sign a lie?

Objectives

  • Understand the end of the play
  • Explore integrity, honour and public image
  • Present a two minute exposé

Warm-up

Students complete: "My name means... to me." Then: what is a reputation? Can you lose it in one day?

Documents

Document 4: Act IV. Autumn 1692. Abigail has run away with Parris's money. Rebecca Nurse and John Proctor are to be hanged. Hale begs the prisoners to confess and live. Proctor first agrees to confess, but when Danforth wants his signed confession nailed to the church door, he tears the paper. He goes to his death; Elizabeth refuses to plead with him to change his mind.
"Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, John Proctor
"How may I live without my name? I have given you my soul; leave me my name!"
Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, John Proctor

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 4: Act IV: Because it is my name!

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Arthur Miller, The Crucible, Act IV, with Document 4

  • “Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!” (Act IV, John Proctor)
  • “How may I live without my name? I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” (Act IV, John Proctor)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 4What strikes you first?
“Proctor first agrees to confess, but when Danforth wants his signed confession nailed to the church door, he tears the paper” (Document 4).
The turning point is not the confession itself but its public use: his name on the church door.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesAct IVWhich clues? In which line?
Repetition: “Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!” (Act IV).
The name is his identity, his honour and what he leaves to his sons: he has only one.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandAct IVWhat effect? What contrast?
Contrast: “I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” (Act IV).
He gives up his soul to a lie, then refuses to give his name: reputation becomes integrity, the refusal to betray himself and the others.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 4What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Elizabeth will beg him to sign and live.
Not confirmed: “Elizabeth refuses to plead with him to change his mind” (Document 4).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningAct IVWhich interpretation do I defend?
“How may I live without my name?” (Act IV).
Proctor, a flawed man, becomes a tragic hero: he chooses death rather than a public lie that would betray the other prisoners and himself.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

Lesson 5: Salem and McCarthyism

Part 5. Why did Arthur Miller use 1692 to speak about the America of the 1950s?

Objectives

  • Understand McCarthyism and the HUAC
  • Read short extracts from Miller's 1996 essay
  • Compare Salem and the Red Scare

Warm-up

Students see the word blacklist. What could it mean? What would happen to you if your name were on it?

Documents

Document 5: the Red Scare.
  • After 1945, the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union creates a fear of communist spies.
  • In February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy claims he has a list of communists working in the State Department.
  • The House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) questions writers, actors and directors. They are asked to "name names". Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood.
  • In March 1954, the journalist Edward R. Murrow criticises McCarthy on his CBS programme See It Now. In December 1954, the Senate censures McCarthy.
  • In June 1956, Arthur Miller appears before HUAC and refuses to name others. He is convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957; the conviction is overturned in 1958.
"“The Crucible” was an act of desperation."
Arthur Miller, “Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’”, The New Yorker, October 1996
"Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth."
Arthur Miller, “Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’”, The New Yorker, October 1996
Easy to find: "What is McCarthyism? And how did it happen?", Ellen Schrecker, TED-Ed; the film Good Night, and Good Luck (2005).

The full spirale de Gorse · Lesson 5: Salem and McCarthyism

The first turn always starts from what strikes you. On each turn, the idea is outside the spiral and the line from the text is inside. Four turns, then the pointe. Your oral keeps turns 1, 2 and 5.

Text studied: Document 5 “the Red Scare”, with Arthur Miller, “Why I Wrote ‘The Crucible’”, The New Yorker, October 1996

  • “They are asked to “name names”. Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood.” (Document 5)
  • ““The Crucible” was an act of desperation.” (Arthur Miller, The New Yorker, 1996)
  • “Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth.” (Arthur Miller, The New Yorker, 1996)

Station table

StepQuestionAnswerReasoningWhat I learn
1 Je remarque · I noticeDoc. 5What strikes you first?
HUAC questions writers, actors and directors: “They are asked to ‘name names’” (Document 5).
Like the girls of Salem, witnesses must accuse others to save themselves.
Start from what strikes you.
2 Je repère · I spot the cluesDoc. 5Which clues? In which line?
“Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood” (Document 5).
Refusing costs a career, as refusing to confess cost a life in Salem: the pressure is the same.
Quote each clue with its reference.
3 Je comprends · I understandMiller, 1996What effect? What contrast?
“‘The Crucible’ was an act of desperation” (Miller, 1996).
Miller could not attack McCarthy openly, so he wrote an allegory: 1692 lets him speak about the 1950s.
Explain the effect of a contrast.
4 J’anticipe · I predictDoc. 5What is my hypothesis? Is it confirmed?
Hypothesis: Miller, like Proctor, will refuse to name others.
Confirmed: “In June 1956, Arthur Miller appears before HUAC and refuses to name others”; he is convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, and the conviction is overturned in 1958 (Document 5).
Check a hypothesis in the text.
5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaningDoc. 5Which interpretation do I defend?
“Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth” (Miller, 1996).
The allegory makes the mechanism visible (fear, accusation, forced confession) and keeps the memory of fear alive for readers who never felt it.
Link the analysis to the key question.

Support sentence: “I can see … in Act … (or in Document …). This shows me … because …”

In pairs, use reliable sites (encyclopaedias, museums, newspapers) to answer. Note the source of each answer.

Answer key
  1. In Wheeling, West Virginia; he claimed to have a list of communists in the State Department.
  2. House Un-American Activities Committee.
  3. Ten Hollywood screenwriters and directors who refused to answer HUAC in 1947 and were jailed and blacklisted.
  4. "Have you no sense of decency, sir?" (9 June 1954).
  5. On 2 December 1954.
  6. Elia Kazan.

    • ““The Crucible” was an act of desperation.” (Arthur Miller, The New Yorker, 1996)

    • Writers were asked to ______.

Check my spiral
  1. 1 Je remarque · I notice (Doc. 5): HUAC questions writers, actors and directors: “They are asked to ‘name names’” (Document 5). Like the girls of Salem, witnesses must accuse others to save themselves.
  2. 2 Je repère · I spot the clues (Doc. 5): “Those who refuse can lose their jobs and be blacklisted in Hollywood” (Document 5). Refusing costs a career, as refusing to confess cost a life in Salem: the pressure is the same.
  3. 3 Je comprends · I understand (Miller, 1996): “‘The Crucible’ was an act of desperation” (Miller, 1996). Miller could not attack McCarthy openly, so he wrote an allegory: 1692 lets him speak about the 1950s.
  4. 4 J’anticipe · I predict (Doc. 5): Hypothesis: Miller, like Proctor, will refuse to name others. Confirmed: “In June 1956, Arthur Miller appears before HUAC and refuses to name others”; he is convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, and the conviction is overturned in 1958 (Document 5).
  5. 5 Je trouve le sens · I find the meaning (Doc. 5): “Fear doesn't travel well; just as it can warp judgment, its absence can diminish memory's truth” (Miller, 1996). The allegory makes the mechanism visible (fear, accusation, forced confession) and keeps the memory of fear alive for readers who never felt it.
